beats.narration_text: Bonjour — Sridhar again. Einstein had shown that light waves can act like particles. In 1924, a doctoral student asked the reverse question: can matter act like a wave? His committee almost rejected the idea. Two years later, a contaminated nickel sample in a New Jersey lab accidentally proved him right.

beats.narration_text: Act one. The wave nobody ordered — and the accident that confirmed it.

props.headline: The Wave Nobody Ordered
props.topic: De Broglie's reversal, and the accident that confirmed it

beats.narration_text: De Broglie's thesis committee nearly rejected it — a wavelength for matter itself. Einstein called it brilliant, and de Broglie won the Nobel Prize. Two years later, Davisson and Germer weren't even testing his idea. Their nickel sample was contaminated. Annealing it to clean up the mess accidentally turned polycrystal into single crystal — and electrons started diffracting like X-rays.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: de Broglie's thesis (λ=h/p) + the Davisson-Germer accident (polycrystal -> single crystal)

beats.narration_text: De Broglie's formula is Einstein's own relation, reversed: wavelength equals h over momentum. For an electron accelerated through V volts, that collapses to a shortcut — 1.226 nanometers over the square root of V. At 150 volts, the wavelength lands at one-tenth of a nanometer — the same spacing as atoms in a solid. That's not a coincidence. That's why electrons can diffract at all.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: lambda = h/p reversal, the electron shortcut formula, 150V -> 0.1nm

beats.narration_text: Davisson and Germer fired 54-volt electrons at nickel and saw a sharp peak at 50 degrees. The de Broglie wavelength at 54 electron-volts: 0.167 nanometers. Feed that into Bragg's law for nickel's crystal planes and you get 66.6 degrees — close, not exact. The gap isn't a failure. It's the crystal's own inner potential, accelerating the electrons slightly, and correcting for it closes the gap completely.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: Bragg diffraction geometry, the golden-test comparison (66.6° predicted vs 50° observed, inner-potential correction)

beats.narration_text: One distinction matters more than the arithmetic. This wavelength is not the electron's size. The classical electron radius is a hundred-millionth of the de Broglie wavelength — eight orders of magnitude smaller. The wavelength describes how the electron moves, not how big it is. A little ball with ripples around it is the wrong picture entirely.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: wavelength vs. classical electron radius, eight orders of magnitude

beats.narration_text: Act two. One electron at a time — and the pattern that shouldn't be possible.

props.headline: One Electron at a Time
props.topic: Tonomura's buildup, and what destroys interference

beats.act: II — One Electron at a Time
beats.narration_text: In 1989, Tonomura's team fired electrons at a biprism one at a time — never more than one in the apparatus at once. Each arrived as a single dot, a single click, exactly like a particle should. Nothing about a lone particle should build an interference pattern. And yet, dot by dot, that is exactly what happened.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: electron gun -> biprism splitting one path into two coherent paths -> single dot on the detector

beats.act: II — One Electron at a Time
beats.narration_text: At ten electrons, the dots look random. At two hundred, faint clusters appear. By six thousand, stripes are forming. By seventy thousand, the picture is unmistakable: bright and dark fringes, the exact pattern a wave predicts for two open paths. Each electron is a particle on arrival. The accumulated dots are a wave's signature.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: the single-electron buildup — dots accumulating into fringes across 10/200/6000/70000 electrons

beats.act: II — One Electron at a Time
beats.narration_text: The rule isn't only for electrons. A buckyball, sixty carbon atoms, still shows fringes in Vienna's diffraction experiments. A person walking at one meter per second has a wavelength of ten to the minus thirty-five meters — twenty-six orders of magnitude smaller than a proton. Quantum mechanics isn't wrong at human scale. The wavelength is just too small for anything to ever measure.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: logarithmic scale bar — electron, buckyball, walking person

beats.act: II — One Electron at a Time
beats.narration_text: What is doing the interfering? Max Born answered in 1926: the wave function itself is not physical — its squared modulus is a probability. The Tonomura dots land exactly where psi-squared predicts, one random click at a time. What the wave function actually means, and why its square gives a probability, is Chapter 3's job — this chapter only shows you that it must exist.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: psi(x) -> |psi(x)|^2 as a probability density, dots scattered under the curve, bridge to Chapter 3

beats.narration_text: Two shapes, one particle. De Broglie's reversal — wavelength equals h over momentum, for anything with momentum — was confirmed by an accident nobody planned. Tonomura's single electrons arrive as particles, one dot at a time, yet build a wave's interference pattern. What's interfering was never really in question after Born: psi-squared is a probability, and it matches the dots exactly.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Pick an accelerating voltage for an electron — try somewhere between 20 and 500 volts. Ask Claude to compute the de Broglie wavelength using the shortcut, 1.226 over the square root of V, in nanometers. Then check: does that wavelength land in the range that can diffract off a crystal, roughly 0.1 to 0.3 nanometers? At what voltage does it stop working?
